clinicalPearls: Autosomal dominant cerebellar ataxia caused by a heterozygous variant in CCDC88C, which encodes the scaffold protein DAPLE, on chromosome 14q32.
Adult-onset, slowly progressive gait and limb ataxia with dysarthria.
Distinctive pyramidal involvement: hyperreflexia, spasticity and extensor plantar responses accompany the cerebellar signs, unlike the purer cerebellar subtypes.
Oculomotor findings include saccadic (broken) smooth pursuit and gaze-evoked nystagmus, and intention tremor is common.
First reported in a Han Chinese family.
MRI shows cerebellar atrophy, sometimes with brainstem or pontine involvement.
Mechanistically linked to hyperactivation of the c-Jun N-terminal kinase (JNK) apoptotic pathway.
Biallelic loss-of-function CCDC88C variants cause a wholly distinct autosomal recessive congenital hydrocephalus, a different mechanism and phenotype from the dominant ataxia.
reference.pathophysiology: SCA40 is caused by a heterozygous variant in CCDC88C, which encodes DAPLE (Dishevelled-associating protein with a high frequency of leucine residues), a scaffold protein that modulates Wnt and planar-cell-polarity signalling and the c-Jun N-terminal kinase (JNK) cascade. The dominant ataxia variant is thought to act as a gain of function that hyperactivates JNK signalling, promoting caspase-dependent apoptosis of cerebellar and brainstem neurons and producing progressive spinocerebellar degeneration with prominent pyramidal features. By contrast, biallelic loss-of-function variants in the same gene disrupt neural-tube and ependymal development to cause congenital hydrocephalus, underscoring the allele- and dose-dependent effects of CCDC88C. No nucleotide repeat expansion is involved.
additionalDifferentials: SCA1 (ATXN1) — dominant ataxia in which pyramidal signs and spasticity are prominent
SCA3 / Machado-Joseph disease (ATXN3) — ataxia with spasticity, pyramidal signs and variable extrapyramidal features
SCA7 (ATXN7) — dominant ataxia, distinguished by retinopathy
Spastic ataxia and hereditary spastic paraplegia with cerebellar features, such as SPG7-related disease
Autosomal recessive spastic ataxia of Charlevoix-Saguenay (SACS)
Acquired posterior-fossa or demyelinating disease presenting with mixed cerebellar and pyramidal signs
additionalInvestigations: MRI of the brain to show cerebellar and possible pontine atrophy and exclude structural or demyelinating lesions
CCDC88C sequencing or a hereditary-ataxia gene panel / exome
Repeat-expansion panel to exclude the common repeat-based subtypes such as SCA1, SCA2, SCA3, SCA6 and SCA7
Nerve conduction studies if a peripheral component is suspected
Acquired-ataxia screen where the diagnosis is uncertain
Genetic counselling and family segregation analysis
redFlags: Rapidly progressive spasticity or bulbar failure
Features of raised intracranial pressure or hydrocephalus, particularly in infants or relatives with biallelic disease
Visual or optic symptoms suggesting an alternative subtype
Sphincter disturbance or a sensory level pointing to a spinal cord lesion
reference.prognosis: The disorder is slowly progressive over years to decades; superimposed spasticity may add to gait disability, but life expectancy is generally preserved.
pitfalls: Mistaking the pyramidal-predominant picture for hereditary spastic paraplegia or multiple sclerosis
Failing to distinguish the dominant ataxia from the recessive congenital hydrocephalus phenotype of the same gene
Assuming a repeat-expansion mechanism and not proceeding to sequencing
Overlooking the family history when cerebellar and pyramidal signs coexist
references: Adams and Victor's Principles of Neurology
Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice
management: With no disease-modifying therapy for this CCDC88C-related ataxia, base care on physiotherapy for gait and balance, occupational therapy, and speech and language therapy
Manage the prominent pyramidal spasticity with physiotherapy, stretching, an antispasticity agent such as baclofen, and botulinum toxin for focal spasticity
Treat intention tremor symptomatically where it impairs function
Institute falls prevention and provide mobility aids, as spasticity compounds the ataxic gait disability
Monitor for bulbar dysfunction with periodic swallow assessment
Offer genetic counselling and family segregation analysis for the autosomal dominant transmission
